question: How many characters are in a boat's Hull Identification Number (HIN)?
choice_a: 12 characters
choice_c: 10 characters
choice_d: 14 characters
explanation: The HIN is a 12-character number, at least 1/4-inch high, permanently attached to the boat.

question: On a standard boat with a transom, where must the Hull Identification Number (HIN) be attached?
choice_a: The center of the console
choice_b: The upper right of the boat's transom
choice_c: The bottom of the hull, forward of the bow
choice_d: Inside the cabin near the helm
explanation: The HIN must be permanently attached to the upper right of the boat's transom (or on the starboard side within two feet of the stern for boats without a transom).

question: Where is the HIN located on a pontoon boat?
choice_a: On the upper right of the transom only
choice_b: On the bow, centered between the pontoons
choice_c: On the aft crossbeam, within one foot of the starboard hull attachment
choice_d: Pontoon boats are exempt from HIN requirements
explanation: Pontoon boats have a visible HIN on the aft crossbeam within one foot of the starboard hull attachment.

question: Which of the following watercraft is exempt from Ohio's registration and titling laws entirely?
choice_a: A 16-foot fishing boat with a 15-horsepower motor
choice_b: A 14-foot boat with a fixed 10-horsepower motor
choice_c: A personal watercraft
choice_d: A paddleboard
explanation: Sailboards, kiteboards, paddleboards and belly boats or float tubes are exempt from registration and titling laws.

question: A title is required before a person may sell, purchase or otherwise acquire which of the following?
choice_a: An outboard motor of 10 horsepower or greater
choice_c: A ship's lifeboat
choice_d: A watercraft owned by a government agency
explanation: No person may sell, purchase, or acquire an outboard motor of 10 horsepower or greater without a certificate of title.

question: A watercraft less than 14 feet long is exempt from Ohio's titling requirement if it has a permanently affixed mechanical means of propulsion of what horsepower?
choice_a: Less than 5 horsepower
choice_c: Less than 15 horsepower
choice_d: Any horsepower, as long as it is under 14 feet
explanation: Watercraft less than 14 feet with a permanently affixed mechanical propulsion of less than 10 horsepower is exempt from the titling requirement.

question: When an individual sells a titled boat in a casual (private) sale, what must the seller do before presenting the title to the buyer?
choice_a: Mail the title directly to the Division of Parks & Watercraft
choice_b: Photograph the HIN and email it to the buyer
choice_c: Complete the transfer section on the back of the title in the presence of a notary public
choice_d: Nothing further is required of the seller
explanation: In a casual sale, the seller must complete the transfer section on the back of the title in the presence of a notary public before presenting it to the buyer.

question: A watercraft less than 14 feet long with a permanently affixed 10-horsepower motor, originally exempt from titling, was purchased on December 15, 1999. What must the owner do before selling it?
choice_a: Nothing -- it remains permanently exempt from titling
choice_b: Only register it, since titling never applies retroactively
choice_c: Destroy the boat rather than sell it, since it cannot legally be transferred
choice_d: Apply to a title office and obtain a title before selling it
explanation: Watercraft less than 14 feet with a permanently affixed mechanical propulsion of 10 horsepower or greater, purchased on or before January 1, 2000, must be titled before the owner sells it, even though it may not have needed a title when purchased.

question: Which watercraft is exempt from Ohio's numbering requirement?
choice_a: A boat numbered by another state and used in Ohio for not more than 60 days
choice_b: A privately owned 20-foot bowrider used exclusively in Ohio
choice_c: A rental pontoon boat operating on an Ohio lake
choice_d: A personal watercraft owned by an Ohio resident
explanation: Watercraft numbered by another state and used in Ohio for not more than 60 days are exempt from Ohio numbering.

question: Canoes, rowboats and inflatable watercraft registered under ORC 1547.54 are handled how, under Ohio's numbering law?
choice_a: They must always be numbered like a powered vessel
choice_b: They are not numbered, but instead display an alternative registration
choice_c: They are completely exempt from any registration or numbering
choice_d: They must be numbered only if operated on Lake Erie
explanation: Canoes, rowboats, and inflatable watercraft registered under section 1547.54 will not be numbered but will instead display an alternative registration.

question: Under Ohio's alternative registration option for manually propelled vessels, what does an owner receive if they choose NOT to have the vessel numbered?
choice_a: A square tag and a lower registration fee
choice_b: No tag at all, since the vessel is unregistered
choice_c: A rectangular tag and a higher registration fee
choice_d: A temporary paper permit valid for one boating season only
explanation: An owner who chooses not to have the vessel numbered pays a higher registration fee and obtains a rectangular tag.

question: A boater using the alternative registration option for a manually propelled vessel is stopped and asked to prove registration. How long do they have to produce the valid registration certificate?
choice_a: 24 hours
choice_c: 30 days
choice_d: 72 hours
explanation: Boaters with an alternative registration have 72 hours to produce the valid registration certificate.

question: Under federal documentation rules referenced in the guide, roughly how long must a boat be to be eligible for U.S. Coast Guard documentation (at least five net tons)?
choice_a: Roughly 25 feet or more
choice_c: Roughly 20 feet or more
choice_d: Roughly 40 feet or more
explanation: Boats must be at least five net tons to be eligible for documentation, which is roughly 25 feet or more in length.

question: A documented vessel operating in Ohio must do what regarding state registration?
choice_a: It is completely exempt from any Ohio registration
choice_b: It must still be registered in Ohio and display two Ohio tags, but is exempt from numbering
choice_c: It must display an Ohio number but no tags
choice_d: It must be re-documented annually with the state of Ohio
explanation: Documented vessels must be registered in Ohio and display two Ohio tags, but are exempt from numbering.

question: What is the correct format for a traditionally registered Ohio watercraft number?
choice_a: "OH" followed by two letters and then four numbers
choice_b: Six numbers with no state prefix
choice_c: "OH" followed by four numbers and then two letters
choice_d: "OHIO" spelled out, followed by six numbers
explanation: The traditional registration number is displayed as "OH" followed by four numbers and two letters, e.g. OH 1234 AB.

question: What is the minimum height required for the block characters of a traditional Ohio watercraft number?
choice_a: One inch
choice_c: Four inches
choice_d: Three inches
explanation: The identification number must be in block characters of good proportion, a minimum of three inches in height.

question: Where should the two traditional registration tags be affixed on a numbered boat?
choice_a: On each side of the bow, six inches toward the stern from the number
choice_b: On the stern, one on each side
choice_c: On top of the console, facing upward
choice_d: Inside the boat, near the operator's seat
explanation: The owner shall securely affix the tags on each side of the bow, six inches toward the stern from the number.

question: How long are Ohio watercraft registration certificates and tags valid for, and when do they expire?
choice_a: One year, expiring December 31
choice_b: Up to three years, expiring March 1 of the indicated year
choice_c: Five years, expiring on the owner's birthday
choice_d: They never expire once issued
explanation: Registration certificates and tags, including alternative registrations, are valid for up to three years and expire on March 1 of the year indicated.

question: Under Ohio's PFD law, a non-commercial watercraft 16 feet or greater in length must carry which of the following, at minimum?
choice_a: One throwable PFD only, regardless of the number of persons aboard
choice_b: Two wearable PFDs total, regardless of the number of persons aboard
choice_c: One wearable PFD per person, plus one throwable PFD
choice_d: No PFDs are required if all occupants are strong swimmers
explanation: Non-commercial watercraft 16 feet or greater must carry one wearable PFD per person, plus one throwable PFD.

question: A canoe of any length must carry what PFD equipment under Ohio law?
choice_a: One wearable PFD per person plus one throwable PFD
choice_b: No PFDs are required for canoes
choice_c: Only a throwable PFD is required
choice_d: One wearable PFD per person
explanation: Watercraft less than 16 feet in length, and canoes or kayaks of any length, must carry one wearable PFD per person (no throwable PFD requirement).

question: A commercial vessel 26 feet in length or longer must carry which additional item beyond its regular PFD requirement?
choice_a: At least one throwable ring life buoy
choice_c: A life raft rated for twice the vessel's capacity
choice_d: An extra fire extinguisher for every 10 feet of length
explanation: Commercial vessels 26 feet in length or longer must carry at least one throwable ring life buoy in addition to other applicable PFD requirements.

question: Under Ohio's child PFD law, a child under what age must wear a PFD aboard a vessel under 18 feet long?
choice_a: Under 6 years of age
choice_c: Under 12 years of age
choice_d: Under 16 years of age
explanation: No person shall operate a vessel under 18 feet long with a child less than 10 years of age on board unless the child is wearing a PFD.

question: Which statement about inflatable PFDs is accurate, per the guide?
choice_a: They are approved for use with personal watercraft
choice_b: They are recommended for children younger than 16 years of age
choice_c: They are not designed for water sports like water skiing or whitewater boating
choice_d: They function as throwable flotation devices
explanation: Inflatable PFDs are not for water sports like water skiing or whitewater boating, not for use with personal watercraft, not for children younger than 16, and are not throwable flotation devices.

question: A water skier being towed behind a boat must wear what type of PFD under Ohio law?
choice_a: Any USCG-approved wearable PFD, including a competition vest
choice_b: No PFD is required as long as the observer is watching closely
choice_c: An inflatable PFD only
choice_d: A USCG-approved wearable PFD specifically designed for water skiing
explanation: A skier must wear a USCG-approved wearable PFD specifically designed for water skiing; competition vests are NOT USCG approved and cannot substitute.

question: Besides a PFD designed for water skiing, what alternative may a barefoot skier wear to comply with Ohio law?
choice_a: A wetsuit specifically designed for barefoot skiing
choice_c: A life ring towed alongside the skier
choice_d: No alternative is permitted -- a ski PFD is always mandatory
explanation: A barefoot skier must wear an effective USCG-approved wearable PFD specifically designed for water skiing, or a wetsuit specifically designed for barefoot skiing.

question: How is a "personal watercraft" (PWC) defined under Ohio law?
choice_a: Any vessel under 20 feet in length with an inboard motor
choice_b: A vessel less than 16 feet long, propelled by machinery, designed to be operated by a person sitting, standing or kneeling on it rather than inside it
choice_c: Any vessel that can exceed 30 miles per hour
choice_d: A vessel with no permanent seating
explanation: A personal watercraft is a vessel less than 16 feet in length, propelled by machinery and designed to be operated by an individual sitting, standing or kneeling on the vessel rather than sitting or standing inside the vessel.

question: A vessel less than 14 feet in length is exempt from which required-equipment rule?
choice_a: The requirement to carry a PFD for each person
choice_b: The requirement to carry a fire extinguisher, regardless of engine type
choice_c: The requirement to carry an anchor and line
choice_d: The requirement to display navigation lights at night
explanation: Vessels less than 14 feet in length, canoes/kayaks, rowing/sculling shells, and sailboats less than 21 feet are exempt from the anchor and line requirement.

question: What anchor scope (rode-to-depth ratio) does the guide describe as generally too short, such that the anchor may not hold?
explanation: A 2:1 scope is described as too short -- the anchor may not hold. 5:1 or more is for calm conditions, and 10:1 or more is for rougher conditions.

question: A disposable fire extinguisher must be removed from service by what date, counting from the date stamped on the bottle?
choice_a: December 31 of the 12th year
choice_c: December 31 of the 10th year
choice_d: December 31 of the 15th year
explanation: Disposable fire extinguishers are good for 12 years from the date stamped on the bottle and must be removed from service on December 31 of the 12th year.

question: A powercraft between 26 and less than 40 feet in length with NO fixed fire extinguishing system in the machinery space must carry how many 5-B portable fire extinguishers, at minimum?
explanation: Per the fire extinguisher table, a vessel 26 or more but less than 40 feet without a fixed fire extinguishing system must carry 2 portable 5-B extinguishers (1 if a fixed system is present).

question: How many 5-B portable fire extinguishers may a single 20-B portable fire extinguisher substitute for?
choice_a: One 5-B extinguisher
choice_c: Two 5-B extinguishers
choice_d: Four 5-B extinguishers
explanation: One 20-B portable fire extinguisher may be substituted for two 5-B portable fire extinguishers.

question: A powercraft less than 26 feet in length is exempt from the fire extinguisher requirement if it meets which combination of conditions?
choice_a: It is painted a bright, high-visibility color
choice_c: It has an inboard motor and enclosed cabin
choice_d: Designed for an outboard motor, open construction, cannot entrap explosive/flammable gases, and does not carry passengers for hire
explanation: A powercraft less than 26 feet, designed for an outboard motor, of open construction, not capable of entrapping explosive/flammable gases or vapors, and not carrying passengers for hire, is exempt from the fire extinguisher requirement.

question: On Lake Erie and its immediately connecting bays, harbors and anchorage areas, a vessel 16 feet or more in length must carry which distress signals at all times?
choice_a: Both day and night visual distress signals
choice_c: Day signals only
choice_d: No distress signals are required on Lake Erie
explanation: On Lake Erie and connecting waters, vessels 16 feet or more (or carrying six or fewer passengers for hire) must carry both day and night visual distress signals at all times.

question: On Ohio waters OTHER than Lake Erie and its connecting bays/harbors/anchorage areas, what daytime distress signal meets the minimum requirement?
choice_a: A handheld air horn
choice_c: A red flare
choice_d: A whistle blast pattern
explanation: On other Ohio waters, no person shall operate without an approved daytime distress signal -- an orange distress flag meets the minimum requirement.

question: Which vessel is exempt from carrying a distress signal on Ohio waters other than Lake Erie?
choice_a: A 40-foot cruiser
choice_c: A sailboat less than 26 feet in length with completely open construction
choice_d: A commercial vessel carrying passengers for hire
explanation: Vessels competing in an organized marine event, manually propelled vessels, or sailboats less than 26 feet with completely open construction are exempt from carrying a distress signal.

question: Which item is required on every gasoline engine installed in a vessel, EXCEPT an outboard motor, to control backfire flame?
choice_a: A carbon monoxide detector wired to the ignition
choice_c: An enclosed engine compartment with no ventilation
choice_d: A backfire flame arrestor, securely attached with a flame-tight connection
explanation: Every gasoline engine installed in a vessel, except an outboard motor, must be equipped with an acceptable backfire flame control device, securely attached to the air intake with a flame-tight connection.

question: Powercraft using gasoline with a flashpoint of less than 110°F must have ventilation consisting of at least how many ventilators fitted with cowls (or the equivalent)?
choice_a: Two
choice_c: Three
choice_d: Four
explanation: At least two ventilators fitted with cowls or their equivalent are required for properly ventilating the bilges of every engine and fuel tank compartment.

question: Under Ohio's muffler noise limits, what is the maximum decibel level measured in a stationary sound level test at one meter with the engine at low idle speed (per SAE J2005)?
choice_a: 75 decibels
choice_c: 80 decibels
choice_d: 85 decibels
explanation: No person shall operate a powercraft exceeding 90 decibels on the "A" scale in a stationary sound level test prescribed by SAE J2005.

question: What is the maximum decibel level for a powercraft measured from shoreline in any level of operation, per SAE J1970?
choice_a: 65 decibels
choice_c: 75 decibels
choice_d: 90 decibels
explanation: No person shall operate a powercraft exceeding 75 decibels on the "A" scale measured as specified by SAE J1970, from shoreline with the boat in any level of operation.

question: A vessel of 12 meters (39.4 feet) or more in length must be provided with which sound signal equipment?
choice_a: A bell only
choice_b: An air horn only, no bell required
choice_c: No sound equipment is required if the vessel has VHF radio
choice_d: A power whistle or power horn and a bell
explanation: A vessel of 12 meters (39.4 feet) or more in length shall be provided with a power whistle or power horn and a bell.

question: What size oil pollution placard must vessels 26 feet or more display near the engine or bilge pump controls?
choice_a: 5 by 8 inches
choice_c: 8 by 10 inches
choice_d: 10 by 12 inches
explanation: Vessels 26 feet or more must display a 5-inch by 8-inch oil pollution placard near the engine or bilge pump controls.

question: What is suitable as a portable means of discharging oily waste on a recreational vessel, per the guide?
choice_a: A garden hose
choice_c: A shop vacuum
choice_d: There is no portable option -- a fixed system is always required
explanation: A bucket or bailer is suitable as a portable means of discharging oily waste to a reception facility on recreational vessels.

question: Vessels 26 feet or longer must display a garbage discharge placard of what minimum size, with lettering at least 1/8-inch high?
choice_a: 3 by 6 inches
choice_c: 4 by 9 inches
choice_d: 8 by 16 inches
explanation: Vessels 26 feet or longer must display a durable placard at least 4 by 9 inches in size, with lettering at least 1/8-inch high.

question: Self-propelled vessels of what minimum length must carry a copy of the Inland Navigation Rules on board?
choice_a: 16 meters (52.5 feet) or more
choice_c: 26 feet or more
choice_d: 12 meters (39.4 feet) or more
explanation: Operators of self-propelled vessels 12 meters (39.4 feet) or more in length must carry on board a copy of the Inland Navigation Rules.

question: Except on Lake Erie, the Muskingum River and the Ohio River, what must be done with a vessel's sink, toilet or sanitary system capable of discharging waste into state waters?
choice_a: It must be removed, sealed, or made to drain into a holding tank that can be pumped ashore
choice_b: It may be used freely as long as the waste is filtered first
choice_c: It may only be used between sunset and sunrise
choice_d: It must be replaced with a chemical toilet before every outing
explanation: Such a sink, toilet, or sanitary system must be removed, sealed, or made to drain into a tank or reservoir that can be carried or pumped ashore for disposal.

question: On a vessel with a Type I, II, or III Marine Sanitation Device (MSD) fitted with a "Y" valve, what must be done to prevent illegal overboard discharge?
choice_a: The valve must be left fully open at all times
choice_b: The valve must be secured with a lock or non-releasable seal, or the handle removed
choice_c: The valve must be painted a bright color for visibility
choice_d: Nothing -- Y-valves are self-regulating
explanation: "Y" valves that direct waste overboard must be secured so the valve cannot be opened for discharge -- by a lock or non-releasable seal, or by removing the handle.

question: Vessels 65 feet and under with installed toilet facilities operating on Lake Erie, the Muskingum River or the Ohio River may use which type of Marine Sanitation Device?
choice_a: Only a Type I MSD
choice_b: Any commercially available toilet, certification is not required
choice_c: A U.S. Coast Guard certified Type I, II, or III MSD
choice_d: None -- installed toilets are prohibited on vessels this size
explanation: Vessels 65 feet and under may use a U.S. Coast Guard certified Type I, II or III MSD.

question: A PFD carried aboard a vessel must meet which set of requirements under Ohio law?
choice_a: Any color, as long as it floats
choice_c: Stored in a locked compartment for safekeeping
choice_d: USCG approved, good/serviceable condition, appropriate size, readily accessible at all times
explanation: Each PFD must be U.S. Coast Guard approved, in good and serviceable condition, an appropriate size for the wearer, and readily accessible to each person aboard at all times.

question: What is required of a PWC operator whose personal watercraft is equipped by the manufacturer with a lanyard-type engine cutoff switch?
choice_a: The lanyard must be attached to the person, their clothing, or their PFD as appropriate
choice_b: The lanyard is optional equipment and need not be attached
choice_c: The lanyard must be tied to the steering column instead
choice_d: The lanyard is only required for operators under age 18
explanation: A person operating a PWC equipped with a lanyard-type engine cutoff switch must attach the lanyard to the person, the person's clothing, or PFD as appropriate.
